title: A Dusty, Barn-Find Bizzarrini Shines at Retromobile NY

body_markdown:
At the back of the Jacob Javits Convention Center in New York City, where beautiful classic cars were arranged in rows ahead of the Gooding Christie’s Retromobile auction, one rare 1967 Bizzarrini stood out. It was covered in dirt; its paint was cracked like a dry lakebed, and the dusty interior looked like it had been ravaged by wet bears.


Except for having air in its tires, this 5300 GT Strada looked much as it did the day it was pulled from the garage in Michigan earlier this year, where it had spent decades. On Friday afternoon, this ultimate project car[sold for $687,000, including auction fees](https://www.goodingco.com/lot/1967-bizzarrini-5300-gt-strada?filtersInput%5BauctionType%5D%5B0%5D=Live%20Auction&filtersInput%5BauctionYear%5D%5B0%5D=2026&filtersInput%5BliveAuctionVenue%5D%5B0%5D=R%C3%A9tromobile%20New%20York&sortBy=ENDING_SOONEST&pageNumber=2) .


Peter Valdez-Dapena


Peter Valdez-Dapena


Peter Valdez-Dapena


Peter Valdez-Dapena


For its new owner, whose identity was not revealed, turning this car back into what it once was will take another $400,000 to $700,000, said Gooding Christie’s Senior Specialist David Brynan.


It could well be worth the cost, though. A Bizzarrini 5300 GT Strada is a rare car shrouded in mystery. No one knows for sure how many were made or where they all are, so the discovery of this one was, by itself, an important event.


Peter Valdez-Dapena


The 5300 GT was developed by Giotto Bizzarrini, who had earlier, when he worked at Ferrari, helped engineer the 250 GTO, which is today one of the world’s most valuable automobiles. He left Ferrari in the winter of 1961 and, the next year, began working on new cars with the industrialist Renzo Rivolta under Rivolta’s Iso brand. It was under this relationship that Bizzarrini began work on the Iso Grifo A3/C.


It was the Grifo, with its body designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro, that Bizzarrini developed into the Bizzarrini 5300 GT. The essential formula remained unchanged, with a Chevrolet 327 V-8 mounted far back under the hood, so far back that some engine work had to be done through an opening in the passenger compartment. Under the Iso Grifo name, it won its class at Le Mans in 1965, finishing ninth overall.


Iso Grifo A3/C during the 24 Hours of Le Mans at Circuit de la Sarthe on June 19, 1965.


David Phipps/Sutton Images


It came in different types for slightly different purposes, and the cars were updated over time. The car Gooding Christie’s sold was a second-series 5300 GT Strada. It came with modern amenities like power windows and a Voxson radio. It also retained its wood-rimmed steering wheel that still looks much nicer than its surroundings.


Gooding Christie's


Gooding Christie's


The Strada version of the 5300 GT came with a single four-barrel carburetor attached to its 350-horsepower L79 Corvette engine and a four-speed manual transmission. 5300 GT Corsa models came with four twin-choke carburetors and could produce about 400 horsepower. They also had stiffer race-tuned suspension and generally less nicely equipped interiors.


Gooding Christie's


Less expensive fiberglass-bodied versions were also made. These were called the 5300 GT America.


While speed and performance were priorities at Bizzarrini, record-keeping was not. That’s why it’s hard to pin down a precise number of 5300 GTs ever made, but Gooding Christie’s puts it at “approximately 125,” including both the 5300 GT itself and the earlier Iso Grifo A3/C.


This particular Bizzarrini was first owned by Giangiacomo Elia, an actor living in Rome who appeared in movies like 1971’s “Slaughter Hotel” (Italian title: “ *La bestia uccide a sangue freddo* ”) *.*


It went through several other Italian owners before being exported around 1971 to America into the ownership of a man named Kenneth Ray Caldwell. At some point, it ended up in that Michigan garage under a tarp and some boxes.


Courtesy Gooding Christie's


The car’s subsequent owner, a Bizzarrini enthusiast whom Gooding Christie’s wouldn’t name, was alerted to its presence and was able to negotiate its purchase and rescue.


The car’s history was solidly recreated thanks to some detective work. That can be especially important with these often poorly documented cars, said Brynan.


“We were actually able to trace through an archivist that we work with using the serial number and an old photo that was in the file,” he said. “There’s a black and white photo in the file where you can see the car’s Italian registration record. That was how we were able to get the Italian road registration documents for the car.”


Gooding Christie's


That photograph allowed them to dig down even more.


“With those documents, we were able to get the entire ownership history, build date, all that kind of stuff, and trace all that. So we have all those documents now,” he said in an interview the day before the sale.


Given the car’s history, he said, its new owner may not want to restore it all. They might just put it on display as it is, just like Gooding Christie’s did at Retromobile New York, dirt, rust, and all. It is, after all, a car with a story, and all that is part of it.


Gooding Christie's
